summary: Defines a common framework and XML format for writing rules about who may see application-specific data, such as a person's location or presence. Other documents can extend the rule language for their own needs.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a note on your door saying who may come in and who may peek at where you are. This is a shared way to write those notes so many different apps can read the same rules.

questions: how to express privacy rules in xml
what is common policy for presence and location
how do presence authorization rules work
what is the sphere condition in common policy
how are common policy permissions combined
subtitle: A shared XML format for rules about who may see your presence or location, built to be extended.

tldr.problem: Presence and location systems each needed rules about who may see a person's data, and those rules were being designed separately.
tldr.mechanism: Common Policy defines an XML rule set. Each rule has conditions (identity, sphere, validity), actions and transformations, and all matching rules are combined by union so that rules only ever grant permissions.
tldr.outcome: Application-specific documents extend the framework with their own conditions, actions and transformations, and must define them so that the combining rules do not lower privacy protection.

today: RFC 4745 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2007. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It serves as the base for presence and location policy documents.

sections.title: A Framework for Access Rules
sections.content:
RFC 4745 defines a framework for authorization policies that control access to application-specific data. It came from combining the common parts of two authorization systems that had been developed separately, one for presence and one for location. Sharing the mechanism makes presence more valuable when combined with location, and encourages a generic, extensible framework.

The framework is meant to be enhanced by domain-specific policy documents, for example for presence and location. It is not limited to those two domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different apps both needed rules about who can see what. Instead of writing two rule books, they share one and each adds its own pages.

sections.title: Roles and Modes of Operation
sections.content:
The RFC names four roles. The Presentity / Target (PT) is the entity the information is about. The Rule Maker (RM) creates the authorization rules. The Policy Server (PS) has access to both the rules and the data. The Watcher / Recipient (WR) asks for the data.

The PS gets a query through a 'using protocol', learns the authenticated identity of the WR, finds the matching rules, combines them and returns data filtered accordingly. Three modes are covered: passive request-response (the PS is the responder, as with HTTP or LDAP), active request-response (the PS contacts the WR, as with a SIP INVITE), and event notification, which adds a subscription phase. One rule set schema serves all three.
sections.plainLanguage: There is you (the target), the person who writes your rules, a doorkeeper who knows the rules and has your information, and a visitor who asks. The doorkeeper checks the rules before telling the visitor anything.

sections.title: Design Goals and Non-Goals
sections.content:
The goals shape the format. Each rule must be representable as a row in a relational database. Rules are permit only: removing a rule can never increase permissions, and the order of rules does not matter. Permissions are additive, so if several rules match, the WR gets the union. The format must be upgradeable without breaking servers that are not upgraded, and it must give no false assurance: rules based on weekday and time-of-day ranges were avoided because they are easy to misread, for instance around time zones.

Non-goals for this first version: external references from rules, regular expressions or partial matches such as glob patterns, and repeat times. The validity element, which limits a rule's lifetime, is not a repeat time.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules can only say 'yes, you may see this'. They never say 'no'. Adding another rule can only let more through, never less, which keeps things simple and hard to get wrong.

sections.title: The Rule Set Data Model
sections.content:
A rule set holds zero or more rules in no particular order. Each rule has an id chosen by the rule maker, which MUST NOT be reused for two rules available to the PS at the same time for a given PT. A rule has three parts: conditions, actions and transformations.

All conditions in a rule must be TRUE for it to apply. Actions and transformations together are the permission. Transformations change the data before it reaches the WR, for example by lowering the precision of a location. Actions cover every other operation. Both are defined by application-specific extensions, and the framework has no deny.

The union of permissions acts as a mask over the real data. If the WR asked for only a subset, such as city-level location, the result MUST be the intersection of what was granted and what was requested. Extensions MUST define their own namespace and cannot change this schema.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule is an 'if' and a 'then'. If the visitor matches, then show them this much. All the matching rules are stacked up, and the visitor sees whatever any of them allows.

sections.title: Conditions: Identity, Sphere and Validity
sections.content:
The identity condition matches authenticated entities only. If it is absent, identity is ignored and the rule applies to anyone. <one id='...'/> matches exactly one identity, written as a URI. <many/> matches any authenticated user, or any user in a given domain, and <except> children exclude individual ids or whole domains. Domain comparison translates percent-encoding, converts to ASCII per RFC 3490, and compares each label.

The sphere condition matches when the target is in a stated state such as work, home, meeting or travel. Its value may hold several blank-separated tokens, which are ORed, compared case-insensitively as opaque strings. The validity condition holds from and until pairs in XML dateTime format; it is true when the current time is at or after a from and before the matching until. The server does not delete expired rules.

Sub-elements of conditions combine with logical AND. An unknown-namespace condition, or an unknown child of identity, evaluates to FALSE.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule can say who it is for (one person, or everyone from one place except a few), what mood or place you are in (work, home), and for how long it counts.

sections.title: Combining Permissions
sections.content:
A request is matched against every rule. Rules whose conditions are all TRUE form the matching rule set, and each type of permission is combined separately by its data type. A missing value counts as the lowest possible value for its type.

  • Boolean: TRUE if at least one matching rule says TRUE.
  • Integer, real and date-time: the maximum value.
  • Set: the union.

The RFC's worked example has six rules and a query from bob at 2003-12-24T17:15:00+01:00 while the sphere is work. Only rules 3 and 5 fire. The combined result is X = TRUE, Y = 12 (the maximum of 3 and 12) and Z = o, the maximum of two levels.
sections.plainLanguage: When several rules say yes to different things, the visitor gets the biggest answer from each category, never less than any single rule allows.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Security considerations depend largely on the application data, so extending documents must cover them. The one general rule is that new actions and transformations, with their allowed values, must be defined so that the combining rules of Section 10 do not lower the level of privacy protection. Meta policies, which decide who may change a rule set, are outside the scope of this document.

IANA registrations cover the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:common-policy, the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:common-policy and the media type application/auth-policy+xml. The media type carries authorization policies, so precautions should limit disclosure of that information.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone adding new kinds of rules must make sure that stacking rules together never leaks more than the owner meant. Who may edit the rules is a separate question this document leaves open.
